The experiments were conducted in the Alice C. Tyler recirculating water flume at the University of Washington.
The free stream velocity was 1.1 m/s, the dynamic depth was 0.48 m, and the water temperature was 38.9 ± 0.1°C.
The diameter-based Reynolds number (Re_D) ranged from 1.6 × 10^5 to 2.7 × 10^5, and the Froude number (Fr_h) was 0.51.
The blade height (h) was 23.4 cm, and the outermost diameter (D_o) was approximately 17.2 cm.
The blockage ratio was around 11% across all tests.
Positive camber is defined as having an outward concavity away from the turbine axis.
Virtual camber is positioned such that it would have an outward concavity away from the turbine axis throughout the cycle.
Increasing c/R leads to an increase in both virtual camber and virtual incidence.
Increasing toe-out preset pitch (more negative α_p) results in lower performance in the upstream and higher performance in the downstream.
Increasing net camber, either through virtual or geometric camber, increases upstream power production but reduces downstream performance.
The optimal tip-speed ratio ranged from 2.3 to 3.6, with the highest values for low c/R and the lowest for high c/R.
The optimal preset pitch angle was found to be more negative as c/R increased.
The optimal performance at a given net camber occurs at a relatively constant net incidence of 0° to +1°.
The effects of increasing c/R and decreasing optimal λ have opposing effects on the chord-based Reynolds number (Re_c), with the effect of increasing c/R dominating.
The datasets from Hunt et al. and Chi were obtained using the same experimental setup and under similar flow conditions.
